analysis.one_liner: Requires your affirmative permission before credit bureaus can share your credit report.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by two Senate Democrats, was referred to the Banking Committee, never received a vote, and died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: Today, credit bureaus can generally sell or share your credit report unless you tell them to stop (you have to opt out). This bill would flip that: the bureaus could only release your report for a loan or insurance application, or for a firm offer of credit or insurance, if you gave explicit permission first and the bureau verified who you are. It would also bar bureaus from charging you any fees related to your report, require them to take reasonable steps to prevent data breaches like the 2017 Equifax hack, and order government studies on how to better protect the information in consumer files.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone with a credit file — which is nearly every American adult. People would gain control over who sees their credit report, would not pay fees for accessing or freezing their own information, and would be better protected from identity theft after bureau data breaches.

how_it_helps.text: Credit bureaus could only furnish your report for a loan or insurance underwriting, or for a firm offer of credit or insurance, after obtaining your affirmative informed consent and verifying your identity — replacing the current default where sharing is allowed unless you opt out [S2][S3].
Bureaus could not charge consumers any fee for activities connected to furnishing or controlling access to their reports, including freezes and consent management [S2][S3].

Bureaus would have to use commercially reasonable efforts to prevent unauthorized access to consumer reports, following data-security standards under the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act — a direct response to breaches of bureau-held data [S2][S3].

The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau would write rules for a free, easy way (phone or secure online) to give or revoke consent within one business day, and the GAO would report on what additional protections are needed to keep consumer files secure [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The three big credit bureaus (Equifax, Experian, TransUnion) would lose revenue from selling report access and from 'prescreened' marketing lists, and would bear the cost of building consent-verification and security systems. Credit card issuers and insurers that rely on prescreened offers to find customers would lose their main prospecting channel.
analysis.who_pays_short: Credit bureaus and mass credit/insurance marketers

drawbacks.text: Requiring affirmative consent and identity verification before a report can be furnished — even when the consumer initiates a loan or insurance application — could add friction and slow some credit approvals that today happen almost instantly [S3].
Compliance costs for bureaus and lenders, and the loss of prescreening revenue, could be passed back to consumers through higher prices or fewer credit and insurance offers in the mail [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real: giving consumers a veto over who sees their credit file is a meaningful privacy and identity-theft protection, and free access to one's own report removes a genuine irritant. The cost is added friction in a credit system built on instant report pulls, and the burden falls hardest on the bureaus whose business model depends on selling that access. On balance, the protections target a market where consumers currently hold almost no bargaining power.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, read twice, and sent to the Senate Banking Committee, which never took it up — no hearing, no vote, no floor action — and it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Jack Reed introduced the bill on October 23, 2019, with Sen. Chris Van Hollen as the bill's sole cosponsor [S3][S4].
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs — the only action it ever received [S5].
No further action appears in the bill's history: no committee consideration, no floor vote, and no House companion action, and the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit bureaus and the credit-card and insurance marketers who buy prescreened lists are better off, because the opt-in requirement and security mandates that would have curtailed that business never advanced.

for.name: Sen. Jack Reed
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Consumer Credit Control Act of 2019 and made introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (Chair Mike Crapo, R-ID) that never considered the bill
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on October 23, 2019 and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — before the Congress expired.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so there is no record of where members stood; the bill's only recorded support was its two Democratic sponsors, and the committee majority that declined to act was Republican.

industries.note: The bill would force these firms to switch from an opt-out model — where they can share your report unless you stop them — to an opt-in model requiring verified consumer consent, and bars them from charging consumers fees for their own report access. Their revenue depends on selling report pulls and prescreened marketing lists, which the bill directly curtails.

industries.industry: Credit card issuers and insurers using prescreened firm offers
industries.note: Mass 'pre-approved' credit and insurance offers are built on bureaus furnishing lists of consumers without individual consent. The bill would allow those offers only with the consumer's affirmative permission, sharply shrinking this acquisition channel.

industries.industry: Consumers' data-security costs borne by bureaus
industries.note: The bill keeps the private credit-bureau model in place while requiring commercially reasonable security efforts and GAO review of further protections — it regulates the bureaus rather than replacing them with a public alternative.
